# Question

**If parents could turn back time, would they still choose to have children?** In 1976 advice columnist Ann Landers posed this question to her readers and received ≈10,000 responses — about 70% said "no." Lock⁵ contrasts this famous result with contemporary random-sample polls of parents.

## Data source

Counts compiled in Lock⁵ (Lock et al. 2021): Landers voluntary column (n = 10,000), Newsday nationwide random sample (n = 1,373), Kansas City Star random sample of KC parents (n = 409). No Lock5 dataset file; Newsday counts reconstructed from the published 91% figure.

# Exploratory analysis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Would do it again — by sampling method (voluntary column vs random samples)"
w = df.pivot_table(index=["study", "method"], columns="response",
                   values="count", aggfunc="sum")
w["phat"] = w["yes"] / (w["yes"] + w["no"])
labels = {"landers_1976": "Ann Landers\n(voluntary column)",
          "newsday_1976": "Newsday\n(random sample)",
          "kc_star_1976": "KC Star\n(random sample)"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.2))
ax.bar([labels[s] for s in w.index.get_level_values("study")], w["phat"],
       color=["#c76c6c", "#8fbf8f", "#8fbf8f"])
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylabel("Proportion answering \"yes\"")
for x, p in enumerate(w["phat"]):
    ax.text(x, p + 0.02, f"{p:.0%}", ha="center")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Methods & results

One-proportion CIs for each sample; two-proportion z-tests with pooled SE for the three pairwise contrasts, each validated with 100k-replicate randomization and bootstrap.

| Sample | Method | "Yes" share |
|---|---|---|
| Ann Landers 1976 | voluntary column | **30.0%** (3,000 / 10,000) |
| Newsday 1976 | random, US parents | 91.0% (1,250 / 1,373) |
| Kansas City Star 1976 | random, KC parents | 93.9% (384 / 409) |

| Comparison | Diff | Test |
|---|---|---|
| Newsday − Landers | +61.0 pp | z = 43.8, p ≈ 0 (randomization p < 1e-5) |
| KC Star − Landers | +63.9 pp | p ≈ 0 |
| KC Star − Newsday | +2.9 pp | p = 0.067 (not significant) |

# Decision

The infamous "70% wouldn't do it again" was pure **voluntary-response bias**: aggrieved readers self-select into writing in. Random samples agree at ~91–94%, and the two random samples are statistically indistinguishable from each other — a textbook demonstration of why sampling method dominates sample size.
